title: Peter by the fire (Mark 14:66–72)
hookLine: a servant girl, a denial, the rooster twice, and Peter breaks down weeping

cards: While Jesus stands before the council upstairs, Mark cuts back to the courtyard below. Peter is there, the one who said earlier that same night, even if everyone else falls away, not I.
When the others fled, he followed, at a distance, right into the high priest's courtyard. That took courage. He's sitting with the servants by a fire, warming himself.
One of the high priest's servant girls walks past, stops, and really looks at him. You were with the Nazarene, she says. You were with Jesus.
Not a soldier, not a judge: a young woman with a job to do, and one sentence.

teach.b: I don't know what you're talking about, Peter says, and he moves out to the gateway. A rooster crows. The girl sees him again and tells the people standing around: this is one of them.
He denies it again. A little later the bystanders try: surely you're one of them, you're a Galilean; they can hear it in his accent.
And Peter, in the King James Bible, "began to curse and to swear, saying, I know not this man of whom ye speak."
Right then the rooster crows a second time, just as Jesus said: before the cock crow twice, thou shalt deny me thrice.

teach.h: WHEN HE THOUGHT THEREON, HE WEPT.
teach.b: Then Mark gives one short, plain sentence: "And when he thought thereon, he wept." The Greek behind when he thought thereon is rare and hard to pin down.
Translators have guessed: he broke down, he threw himself down, he covered his head. Nobody is sure. But the verb for wept is clear, and its tense suggests he kept on weeping.
Notice the timing. Upstairs, Jesus tells the truth, and it will cost him his life. Downstairs, Peter lies to save his.
Mark sets them side by side.
Tradition links Mark's gospel to Peter's own preaching; if so, Peter told this story on himself. He doesn't hide the failure. The weeping is where he starts again.
This week went from perfume, to the upper room, to a garden where he prayed abba, to a kiss, a trial, and now a fire.

how: Christians read Peter's denial in Holy Week, and a rooster became a common symbol of Peter and of repentance, carved on church towers and pictured in art of his weeping.

games.q: you're Peter. the rooster crows a second time, and you remember what he said. what happens next?
o: you leave quietly and go home.
you go upstairs to find him.
games.why: "And when he thought thereon, he wept." Mark keeps Peter's failure in, and Christians often see it as the start of his turning back.

practice: Think of a time you let someone down, or let yourself down, something real but manageable, not the worst thing you've ever done, and instead of explaining it away, let yourself feel sorry for it; if tears come, let them.
Sadness isn't the end of the story: for Peter, it was the turning point. If you pray, you can bring that failure to God as it is.

wordCard.voice: Peter, warming himself by the fire while three denials slip out, and a rooster crows twice. Then he breaks down weeping.

orig.note: Greek: he wept, in a tense that can mean he kept on weeping. the last word of Mark 14.

carryVoice: Your line: he wept. And the story didn't stop there. Day two hundred twenty-four closes the week.
